title: Role of the piano in early bands and two-beat rhythm
summary: Hug describes the piano as background foundation and the accent on the second beat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Would he sit down at the piano?

No, he'd just tell me, well, as we were playing, he'd say, I use F chord next to an A seventh, next to a D seventh here, a D minor, you know. As we were playing, he'd call them out to me, you know. And, well, as I went along, I gradually got to learn the right changes. And then, the melody, you know. But usually, it was usually the chords. I think you brought out a point right before the interview, Dick, about what part the piano played in those days in the band. Because it was kind of lost. Well, of course, the piano, as always, was used as more of a background instrument in those days, and used mostly as a foundation for the blown instruments. And it wasn't too important to play a melody. In fact, the piano man in those days really didn't even have to be a real great soloist. As long as he could play good chords and give a good solid beat and not interfere with what the blown instruments were doing, he was considered to be all right. Of course, if a man could, if a piano man couldn't take a good solo, well, they let him take it. They let him feature a solo. But he didn't have to be a great soloist in those days. And also, just to be a good rhythm man, that was most important.
What kind of rhythms would you use in that?

Well, we used more or less of the old two beat, you know, the strong beat. The strong beat, rather, was in the second beat. I was taught in those days that the first beat on the bass, you know, shouldn't be too heavy, should be exaggerated too much. But that second beat should be the predominant beat. Because they believed in that strong after beat, that strong second beat, you know. And the first beat would be sort of not as strong as the second beat. And that, that, that, that was employed, I employed that type of playing mostly for the first few years that I played. Until later on, we fell into more of a, of a straight four. But we still accented that second beat, where they, where, where I think that the, the term two beat music came in, came in, you know what I mean? They used that, they used that word two beat. But even when playing a four, we still accented that second beat a little bit, which gave it, gave it the impression that we were playing two beat.
